images.caption: Cemetery shrine, Manzanar Japanese internment camp, Owens Valley, California, looking west toward the Sierra Nevada. The inscription is in Japanese and reads 慰霊塔 (ireitõ), meaning "Monument to console the souls of the dead." The inscription on the back reads "August 1943" and "erected by the Manzanar Japanese." The obelisk shrine currently is draped in strings of origami and has offerings of personal items left by survivors and visitors. The park service periodically itemizes and collects these items in order to gauge the changing feelings of visitors.

images.caption: After its closure, Manzanar Internment Camp was dismantled, leaving little trace. In the decades following, work has slowly been done to bring this history to light, including the placement of markers where camp buildings once stood. Seen here, the former location of the camp's Recreation Hall.

images.caption: After its closure, Manzanar Internment Camp was dismantled, leaving little trace. In this image, rows marking different barracks buildings extend into the distance, seen through the window of one of the recreation barrack buildings.

images.filename: Inside one of the recreation barracks at Manzanar.jpg
images.caption: While all original barracks from the Manzanar Internment Camp were dismantled upon closure, the recreation efforts of the last couple decades have led to the installation of era-appropriate barracks, the sort of housing "provided" at the site. The prisoners themselves usually had to install these WWII (then contemporary, of course) military barracks to then live in despite the harsh desert conditions. Seen here, a cot to demonstrate some of the sleep conditions and a capacity marker.
